before.content_html:
“When We Two Parted” — Lord Byron (1816)

Byron describes the pain of a secret love affair that has ended. The poem is about loss, betrayal, and the lasting damage of a broken relationship. The opening — “When we two parted / In silence and tears” — establishes a tone of grief and emotional suppression. The word “silence” suggests the relationship was secret, and the separation was painful but unspoken.

The poem uses pathetic fallacy: “The dew of the morning / Sunk chill on my brow” — the cold dew reflects the speaker’s emotional coldness and grief. “Pale grew thy cheek and cold, / Colder thy kiss” — the metaphor of coldness represents the death of love. The poem ends by circling back to the beginning: “If I should meet thee / After long years, / How should I greet thee? — / With silence and tears.” This cyclical structure suggests the speaker is trapped in grief — nothing has changed.

Key Fact

Byron uses pathetic fallacy (cold dew), metaphor (cold kiss = dead love), and cyclical structure (ending repeats the beginning) to present heartbreak as inescapable and permanent. The secrecy of the affair intensifies the pain — the speaker cannot publicly grieve.

“Love’s Philosophy” — Percy Bysshe Shelley (1820)

Shelley uses natural imagery to argue that all things in nature are designed to come together, so it is unnatural for two lovers to remain apart. The poem is a persuasive argument for physical union. “The fountains mingle with the river / And the rivers with the ocean” — Shelley builds a chain of natural connections, each one flowing into the next. If nature unites, why shouldn’t lovers?

The final lines — “And the sunlight clasps the earth / And the moonbeams kiss the sea: / What is all this sweet work worth / If thou kiss not me?” — use personification (“clasps,” “kiss”) to make nature itself an argument for love. The rhetorical question at the end challenges the beloved directly. Shelley’s tone is playful but insistent — this is not just a love poem but a persuasion poem, using logic and nature to overcome the beloved’s resistance.

The poem has two stanzas of eight lines each. Each stanza builds a list of natural pairings and ends with a direct appeal to the beloved. The regular ABAB rhyme scheme creates a song-like quality that mirrors the “sweet work” of nature. But the final word of each stanza (“me”) disrupts the smoothness — the speaker’s personal desire breaks through the natural philosophy.

Sonnet 29 — Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1845-46)

Barrett Browning writes about the transformative power of love. The speaker describes how thinking of her beloved changes her emotional state from despair to joy. The poem is part of Sonnets from the Portuguese, a sequence written during her secret courtship with Robert Browning. This autobiographical context adds emotional authenticity.

“I think of thee! — my thoughts do twine and bud / About thee, as wild vines, about a tree” — the extended metaphor of vines around a tree presents love as organic and growing, but also potentially suffocating. Barrett Browning complicates the image: she asks the beloved to “burst, shatter, everywhere!” the vines — she wants the real person, not her idealised thoughts of him. The volta comes when she rejects her own fantasies in favour of reality: “I do not think of thee — I am too near thee.”

Key Fact

Barrett Browning’s extended metaphor of vines on a tree presents love as natural but potentially overwhelming. The volta rejects idealised fantasy for real presence — “I do not think of thee — I am too near thee.” Love is about the real person, not a romanticised idea of them.

Byron vs Shelley: Both write about desire, but Byron presents love as loss and pain (“silence and tears”) while Shelley presents it as joyful natural philosophy. Byron’s tone is elegiac; Shelley’s is persuasive.

Shelley vs Barrett Browning: Both use nature imagery, but Shelley sees nature as a model for love, while Barrett Browning sees it as a metaphor for her own feelings. Shelley argues for physical union; Barrett Browning values emotional and spiritual connection.

Byron vs Barrett Browning: Both explore vulnerability in love. Byron is trapped in grief (cyclical structure); Barrett Browning transforms grief into joy (the volta). Byron’s love is dead; Barrett Browning’s is alive and present.

before.content_html:
“Before You Were Mine” — Carol Ann Duffy (1993)

Duffy imagines her mother’s life before she was born — young, glamorous, carefree. The speaker pictures her mother “in your polka-dot dress … on the corner” laughing with friends. The title claims possessiveness: the mother existed “before you were mine” implies the speaker now owns her. Duffy explores how parenthood transforms identity — the mother became “mine” and lost her independent self.

The poem uses vivid sensory details: “Your polka-dot dress blows round your legs. Marilyn.” The full stop before “Marilyn” gives the word the force of revelation — the mother is compared to Marilyn Monroe, suggesting glamour and desirability. The speaker’s tone is admiring but tinged with guilt: “I knew you would dance like that.” She knows her birth changed her mother forever. Key technique: the perspective shift — Duffy writes as a child imagining a past she never witnessed.

Key Fact

The title reveals possessiveness — the speaker claims ownership of the mother. The poem explores how parenthood transforms identity: the mother’s glamorous, independent past was surrendered when she became a mother. The tone blends admiration with guilt.

“Mother, any distance” — Simon Armitage (1993)

Armitage uses the extended metaphor of a measuring tape to explore a son leaving home. The mother holds one end while the son walks away: “You at the zero-end, me with the spool of tape.” The extended metaphor is brilliantly physical — the tape connects them but must eventually break as the son gains independence.

“I reach towards a hatch that opens on an endless sky / to fall or fly” — the son faces the open world. “Fall or fly” captures the uncertainty of independence: it could go either way. The mother’s “fingertips still pinch / the last one-hundredth of an inch” — she holds on as long as possible, reluctant to let go. The poem captures the universal tension between a parent’s desire to protect and a child’s need for freedom.

Day Lewis watches his son walk away to school for the first time. The memory is eighteen years old but “has not worn away” — the pain of separation is permanent. The son is described “like a satellite / Wrenched from its orbit” — the simile suggests the child is being torn from the parent’s gravitational pull. The final lines resolve with acceptance: “How selfhood begins with a walking away, / And love is proved in the letting go.” This paradox — love is proved by releasing, not holding — is the poem’s central wisdom.

“Follower” — Seamus Heaney (1966)

Heaney describes his childhood admiration for his father, a skilled ploughman. The father is presented as physically powerful: “His shoulders globed like a full sail strung / Between the shafts and the furrow.” The simile “globed like a full sail” makes the father seem heroic, almost mythical. The child “stumbled in his hobnailed wake” — clumsy, small, literally following in his father’s footsteps.

The final stanza reverses the poem: “But today / It is my father who keeps stumbling / Behind me, and will not go away.” The roles have switched — the father is now old and dependent, following the son. The verb “stumbling” transfers from child to father. This reversal is both tender and uncomfortable: the son is frustrated (“will not go away”) even as he remembers his own clumsy devotion.

Key Fact

Heaney’s “Follower” reverses roles: the child who once stumbled behind his heroic father now finds the ageing father stumbling behind him. The poem explores how family relationships change over time — and the guilt that comes with finding a parent burdensome.

Duffy vs Heaney: Both explore parent-child relationships through memory. Duffy imagines a past she never witnessed; Heaney recalls a past he lived. Both involve possessiveness and guilt.

Armitage vs Day Lewis: Both explore separation — a child leaving a parent. Armitage writes from the child’s perspective (“fall or fly”); Day Lewis writes from the parent’s (“love is proved in the letting go”). Both capture the tension between protection and freedom.

Heaney vs Day Lewis: Both present fathers, but from opposite directions. Heaney moves from childhood admiration to adult guilt; Day Lewis moves from parental pain to acceptance. Both use physical imagery (ploughing, walking) to embody emotional experience.

before.description: Byron's grief, Hardy's disillusionment, Doshi's long-distance love, and Causley's Eden Rock.
before.content_html:
Loss & Distance — Four Poems

These poems explore what happens when love is lost, ended, or separated by distance or death. Each poet handles absence differently: Byron with grief, Hardy with bitterness, Doshi with quiet connection, and Causley with serene acceptance.

“When We Two Parted” — Byron (Revisited)

Byron’s speaker is trapped in unresolved grief. The cyclical structure (“silence and tears” opening and closing) creates a sense that the pain has not diminished. The poem’s power lies in its restraint: the speaker cannot publicly grieve because the affair was secret. This forced silence intensifies the emotional damage. The half-rhymes (“morning”/“warning”) create a sense of incompleteness, reflecting the unfinished grief.

“Neutral Tones” — Thomas Hardy (1867)

Hardy describes the moment he realised a love affair was over. The setting is bleak: “We stood by a pond that winter day, / And the sun was white, as though chidden of God.” The pathetic fallacy is powerful — the “white” sun suggests something drained of warmth and life, and the phrase “chidden of God” (scolded by God) implies even God has turned away.

The woman’s smile is described as “the deadest thing / Alive enough to have strength to die.” This oxymoron — something both dead and alive — captures the painful zombie-state of a dying relationship. The poem ends with the image returning: “And a pond edged with greyish leaves.” Like Byron, Hardy uses cyclical structure to trap the speaker in the memory of loss.

Key Fact

Hardy’s “the deadest thing / Alive enough to have strength to die” captures the painful state of a relationship that is dying but not yet dead. The oxymoron makes the reader feel the exhaustion and bitterness of love turning to indifference.

“Letters from Yorkshire” — Maura Doshi (2002)

Doshi presents a long-distance relationship sustained by letters. The speaker (in a city) receives news from a man in Yorkshire who describes digging his garden and seeing “the first lapwings.” His physical, outdoor life contrasts with her indoor, desk-bound existence. Yet the letters create a genuine connection: “Is your life more real because you dig and sow?”

The poem questions whether emotional connection can survive physical distance. Doshi’s answer is yes: “our souls tap out messages across the icy miles.” The word “souls” elevates the connection beyond the physical, and the synaesthesia-like image of souls “tapping” messages blends the physical (tapping) with the spiritual (souls), suggesting communication that transcends technology.

Causley imagines his dead parents waiting for him on the other side of a stream — a boundary between life and death. The scene is idyllic: his mother spreads a picnic cloth, his father has “the same suit / Of Survey tweed.” The precise, mundane details (the “H.P. sauce bottle,” the “tin of pears”) make the scene feel real and comforting rather than frightening.

The final lines — “I had not thought it would be like this” — suggest that death is not the terrifying void we fear but a reunion with loved ones. The stream separating the speaker from his parents is a traditional symbol of the boundary between life and death. Causley’s tone is serene, not grief-stricken — he presents death as something gentle and familiar.

Key Fact

Causley uses precise, everyday details (H.P. sauce, tweed suit, tin of pears) to make the afterlife vision feel familiar and safe. Death is not frightening but a return to the warmth and normality of childhood — a reunion rather than an ending.

Byron vs Hardy: Both present the end of love through bleak imagery and cyclical structure. Byron is grief-stricken and secret; Hardy is bitter and disillusioned. Byron’s love was passionate; Hardy’s has drained to nothing.

Doshi vs Causley: Both present love surviving distance or separation. Doshi’s lovers are separated by geography; Causley’s by death. Both suggest that love transcends physical boundaries — but Doshi’s tone is questioning while Causley’s is serene.

Hardy vs Causley: Hardy presents love’s end as bleak and bitter (drained colour, dead smile); Causley presents death as warm and comforting (picnic, familiar details). Opposite emotional responses to loss.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Byron and Hardy both use cyclical structure and pathetic fallacy to present loss — but Byron is grief-stricken while Hardy is bitterly disillusioned.
  • Doshi presents love surviving physical distance through letters and spiritual connection; Causley presents love surviving death through serene, comforting imagery.
  • In comparisons, focus on the emotional tone of each poem’s response to loss, not just the events described.
before.exam_tip_html: When comparing poems about loss, focus on the emotional response to loss, not just the fact that loss occurs. Byron is grieving, Hardy is bitter, Doshi is reflective, Causley is serene. Analysing how each poet responds — and the methods they use to convey that response — is what earns top marks for AO1 and AO2.

before.content_html:
“Porphyria’s Lover” — Robert Browning (1836)

Browning’s dramatic monologue presents a deeply disturbing speaker who murders his lover Porphyria to preserve the perfect moment of her devotion. The poem opens with pathetic fallacy: “The rain set early in tonight, / The sullen wind was soon awake.” The storm mirrors the speaker’s inner turmoil. When Porphyria arrives, she brings warmth and light: she “made the cheerless grate / Blaze up.”

The speaker realises that Porphyria truly loves him: “That moment she was mine, mine, fair, / Perfectly pure and good.” The repetition of “mine” reveals his possessiveness. He then strangles her with her own hair: “I found / A thing to do, and all her hair / In one long yellow string I wound / Three times her little throat around, / And strangled her.” The casual, matter-of-fact tone is chilling. He shows no remorse: “And yet God has not said a word!” — he believes God approves, or at least does not object.

Key Fact

Browning uses the dramatic monologue to expose the speaker’s distorted logic: he murders Porphyria to “preserve” her love. The repetition of “mine” reveals possessiveness, the calm tone reveals psychopathy, and the final line suggests he believes himself justified. Desire here is controlling, violent, and fatal.

“The Farmer’s Bride” — Charlotte Mew (1916)

Mew’s dramatic monologue presents a farmer whose young wife is terrified of him and of physical intimacy. The farmer married her young: “Three Summers since I chose a maid.” The word “chose” suggests she had no say — marriage as transaction, not partnership. When she ran away, the villagers caught her “like a hare” — the simile reduces the wife to a hunted animal.

The wife is described through nature imagery: “like a mouse,” “like a leveret,” “Her eyes, her hair, her hair!” The farmer’s desire is unrequited — she fears him, and he cannot bridge the gap. The final stanza shifts to desperate, almost threatening desire: “Oh! my God! the down, / The soft young down of her, the brown, / The brown of her — her eyes, her hair, her hair!” The fragmented, breathless repetition suggests his self-control is breaking. Mew leaves the ending ambiguous and ominous.

Nagra presents a joyful, playful depiction of desire in a British-Indian marriage. The speaker is a young Sikh shopkeeper who neglects his father’s shop to be with his new wife upstairs. The poem is full of humour and energy: “my bride / she effing at my mum / in all di colours of Punjabi.” The phonetic English (“di” for “the”) creates a distinctive dialect voice that blends Punjabi and English.

The desire here is healthy, mutual, and joyful — a complete contrast to Browning and Mew. The couple share food and domestic life: “vee share in chapatti / vee share in di chutney.” The mundane domestic detail (chapattis) is presented with the same delight as the moonlit description of her face: “my bride / she hav a red crew cut / and she wear a Tartan sari.” Nagra celebrates multicultural British identity and presents desire as fun, equal, and life-affirming.

Key Fact

Three poems, three types of desire: Browning’s is possessive and fatal, Mew’s is frustrated and potentially dangerous, and Nagra’s is mutual, playful, and life-affirming. The exam often asks about “how desire is presented” — these three provide powerful contrasts.

Browning vs Mew: Both use dramatic monologues to reveal speakers whose desire is controlling. Both objectify women. But Browning’s speaker acts (murder); Mew’s is still restraining himself (the ending is ambiguous). Both expose how patriarchal power distorts desire.

Browning vs Nagra: Maximum contrast — Browning’s desire is possessive, violent, and one-sided; Nagra’s is mutual, joyful, and equal. Browning’s woman is silenced (literally killed); Nagra’s wife is loud, funny, and independent.

Mew vs Nagra: Both present marriage, but Mew’s is a prison (the wife is trapped) and Nagra’s is a celebration (the couple choose each other). Mew’s wife is silent and animal-like; Nagra’s wife is vocal and vibrant.

before.content_html:
“Winter Swans” — Owen Sheers (2005)

Sheers presents a couple whose relationship has been strained. They walk in silence after two days of rain — the pathetic fallacy of the storm mirrors their emotional distance. But when they see swans on a lake, something shifts. The swans “porcelain” their necks towards each other, and the couple begins to reconnect.

The poem’s turning point is nature: the swans model devotion (“they mate for life”), and the couple unconsciously mirror them. The final image — “our hands … folded, one over the other, / like a pair of wings settling after flight” — is a simile that connects the human and natural. Their hands “settling” suggests the turbulence is over. The form supports this: the poem is written in tercets (three-line stanzas) throughout — an imbalanced number suggesting discord — except the final stanza, which is a couplet (two lines), mirroring the couple coming back together.

Key Fact

Sheers uses form to mirror content: tercets (three-line stanzas = imbalance/discord) shift to a final couplet (two lines = the couple reunited). The swans model natural devotion, and nature heals the relationship. Pathetic fallacy shifts from storm (distance) to calm (reconciliation).

“Climbing My Grandfather” — Andrew Waterhouse (2000)

Waterhouse uses the extended metaphor of mountaineering to explore getting to know his grandfather. The speaker “climbs” the grandfather’s body as if scaling a mountain: “I decide to do it free, without a rope or net” — he approaches the relationship without safety barriers, making himself vulnerable.

Physical details map onto the climbing metaphor: the grandfather’s “earth-stained hand” becomes a handhold, his “still-beating heart” is discovered at the summit: “knowing / the slow pulse of his good heart.” The adjective “good” is deceptively simple — it suggests moral worth, kindness, and reliability. The word “slow” implies steadiness and age. The journey from base to summit represents deepening emotional knowledge: getting to know someone takes effort, courage, and patience.

Causley’s “Eden Rock” fits the memory and time theme through its gentle re-creation of a childhood scene. The title alludes to the Garden of Eden — a paradise before the Fall, suggesting innocence and perfection. The mundane domestic details (“H.P. Sauce bottle,” “Survey tweed”) anchor the vision in specific, personal memory, making death feel like a return to something known and safe rather than a step into the unknown.

The poem’s pace is slow and deliberate, matching the dreamy quality of the scene. The final line — “I had not thought that it would be like this” — is both a revelation and a comfort. Time dissolves: past, present, and future merge as the speaker approaches the stream (death) with surprising calm.

Key Fact

Waterhouse’s mountaineering metaphor represents the effort of truly knowing someone. The “summit” (the grandfather’s heart) is the emotional core — reaching it requires vulnerability, patience, and physical closeness. The “accurate” heartbeat suggests reliability and trust.

Memory, Time & Connection

These three poems share a focus on how time affects relationships. Sheers shows a relationship healing in the present moment. Waterhouse explores discovery of a person across a lifetime. Causley dissolves time altogether, merging past and present at the threshold of death. All three suggest that love operates across time — it is not confined to a single moment but evolves, deepens, or transcends.

Sheers vs Waterhouse: Both use physical experience to explore emotional connection. Sheers’ couple reconnect through a shared walk (horizontal movement); Waterhouse’s speaker “climbs” to know his grandfather (vertical movement). Both end with discovery: Sheers finds reconciliation, Waterhouse finds the heartbeat.

Waterhouse vs Causley: Both explore grandparental love through physical detail. Waterhouse’s grandfather is alive (the heart still beats); Causley’s parents are dead (but the scene feels alive). Both use mundane detail to make love tangible and real.

before.content_html:
Why Form Matters

In the AQA exam, AO2 rewards analysis of the poet’s methods. Understanding why a poet chooses a sonnet over free verse, or a dramatic monologue over a lyric, is essential for top-band answers. The form of a poem is not decoration — it is part of the meaning.

The Sonnet Tradition

The sonnet is the traditional form for love poetry (14 lines, iambic pentameter). Three poems in the anthology use or subvert the sonnet form:

Sonnet 29 (Barrett Browning) follows the Petrarchan sonnet structure (octave + sestet) with a volta, reflecting the tradition of devoted love poetry. The form matches the content: sincere, structured devotion. Love’s Philosophy (Shelley) is not strictly a sonnet but uses 16 lines with a song-like ABAB scheme — its regular form supports the logical, persuasive argument. Mother, any distance (Armitage) loosely follows sonnet structure but breaks it: the poem is 15 lines, not 14, and the final line runs over — mirroring the son exceeding the mother’s reach, breaking free of the “form” she represents.

Key Fact

Armitage’s 15-line poem breaks the 14-line sonnet convention — the extra line mirrors the son going beyond the mother’s reach. Using a love-poem form for a parent-child relationship subverts expectations. Form becomes a metaphor for breaking free.

Dramatic Monologues

A dramatic monologue gives voice to a single speaker, revealing character through their own words. The reader must read between the lines to see what the speaker cannot (or will not) acknowledge.

Porphyria’s Lover (Browning) uses the dramatic monologue to expose the speaker’s delusion: he describes murder in a calm, rational tone, revealing psychopathy. The form creates chilling irony — the speaker thinks he is justified, but the reader sees madness. The Farmer’s Bride (Mew) uses the same form to show frustrated desire: the farmer’s perspective is the only one we hear, and his wife is silenced. The monologue form itself becomes an act of control.

Climbing My Grandfather (Waterhouse) is written in free verse with no stanza breaks, creating one continuous “climb” up the page. The absence of pauses mirrors the uninterrupted physical effort of mountaineering and the sustained focus of getting to know someone.

Singh Song! (Nagra) uses a playful, irregular form with phonetic dialect, varying line lengths, and an italicised chorus. The loose structure mirrors the joy and spontaneity of the relationship. Letters from Yorkshire (Doshi) uses unrhymed tercets with enjambment, creating a flowing, conversational tone that mirrors the exchange of letters.

Key Structural Techniques

Enjambment (lines running on without punctuation) creates momentum and mirrors flowing emotion: Barrett Browning’s thoughts “twine and bud” across lines. Caesura (mid-line pauses) creates sudden stops: Hardy’s “We stood by a pond that winter day,” pauses before revealing the bleak setting. Stanza breaks can mark shifts in time, mood, or focus: Heaney’s final stanza in “Follower” reverses the entire poem.

Key Fact

Key structural techniques to discuss: enjambment (momentum, flowing thought), caesura (pause, emphasis), volta (turning point in sonnets), cyclical structure (entrapment), stanza shifts (changed perspective). Always link the technique to its effect on meaning, not just identify it.

Pathetic fallacy: Byron (cold dew = grief), Hardy (white sun = drained love), Sheers (storm = discord, calm = reconciliation).

Extended metaphor: Armitage (tape measure = parental bond), Waterhouse (mountaineering = knowing someone), Barrett Browning (vines = overwhelming thoughts).

Simile: Heaney (“globed like a full sail” = heroic father), Day Lewis (“satellite wrenched from orbit” = child leaving), Mew (“like a hare” = wife as prey).

Personification: Shelley (sunlight “clasps,” moonbeams “kiss” = nature as lover).
before.exam_tip_html: Never just identify a technique — always explain its effect. Instead of “Sheers uses a simile,” write: “Sheers’s simile ‘like swans, / settled after flight’ connects the couple’s reconciliation to the natural devotion of swans that mate for life, suggesting their bond is instinctive and enduring.” This analysis earns AO2 marks because it explains how the technique creates meaning.

before.content_html:
The Comparison Question

Paper 2, Section B gives you one named poem (printed on the page) and asks you to compare it with one poem of your choice from the anthology. The question is worth 30 marks: AO1 (12 marks — ideas and comparisons), AO2 (12 marks — language, form, structure analysis), AO3 (6 marks — context). You have approximately 45 minutes. The named poem is open book (printed), but your chosen poem is closed book — you must recall it from memory.

Key Fact

AO1 = 12 marks (ideas, interpretations, comparison). AO2 = 12 marks (methods — language, form, structure). AO3 = 6 marks (context). The majority of marks reward analysis and comparison, not plot summary. AO2 is equally weighted with AO1 — you must discuss methods to access the top band.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem

You must choose wisely. The best comparison poem is one that shares the theme of the question but takes a different approach. Similarities give you connection points; differences give you analytical depth. Prepare 3–4 “go-to” poems that you know well enough to quote from memory.

Prepared pairings save time in the exam. For example: if the named poem is about loss, you might choose “Neutral Tones” (bitter disillusionment) or “Eden Rock” (serene acceptance). If it is about desire, choose “Singh Song!” (joyful) or “Porphyria’s Lover” (possessive). The greater the contrast, the richer the comparison.

Romantic love: Byron + Barrett Browning (grief vs devotion), Shelley + Nagra (persuasion vs celebration).

Loss/distance: Hardy + Byron (bitter vs grief-stricken), Doshi + Causley (physical distance vs death).

Desire/power: Browning + Mew (fatal vs frustrated), Browning + Nagra (possessive vs mutual).

Parent-child: Heaney + Day Lewis (reversal vs letting go), Duffy + Armitage (possessive memory vs leaving home).

Nature: Shelley + Sheers (nature as model for love vs nature reflecting emotion), Byron + Hardy (pathetic fallacy in grief).

Memory/time: Duffy + Causley (imagined past vs afterlife vision), Heaney + Waterhouse (childhood memory vs discovery).

Essay Structure

Introduction (2–3 sentences): State the theme and your argument. Name both poems and their poets. Example: “Both Sheers in ‘Winter Swans’ and Hardy in ‘Neutral Tones’ use pathetic fallacy to present strained relationships, but while Sheers’s couple find reconciliation through nature, Hardy’s speaker remains trapped in bitter disillusionment.”

Body paragraphs (3–4): Each paragraph should discuss both poems, organised around an aspect of the theme (not poem-by-poem). Use comparative connectives: “Similarly,” “In contrast,” “While [Poet A] presents…, [Poet B] suggests…” Each paragraph needs: a point comparing ideas, quotations from both poems, analysis of methods (AO2), and embedded context (AO3).

Key Fact

Structure: Introduction (thesis + both poems named) → 3–4 paragraphs (both poems in every paragraph, organised by aspect of theme) → Conclusion (link to poets’ wider messages). Never write about one poem then the other — weave them together throughout.

Point: State the comparison. “Both poets use natural imagery to present emotional states, but with contrasting outcomes.”

Evidence (Poem 1): Quote from the named poem. “Sheers describes the couple’s hands as ‘like swans, settled after flight.’”

Comment (AO2): Analyse the method. “The simile connects the couple to swans that ‘mate for life,’ suggesting their bond is instinctive and enduring.”

Link to Poem 2: Compare with your chosen poem. “In contrast, Hardy uses pathetic fallacy to present love as drained and lifeless: ‘the sun was white, as though chidden of God.’”

Context: Embed AO3. “Hardy’s Victorian pessimism, shaped by personal disillusionment, contrasts with Sheers’s modern, more optimistic view that relationships can recover.”

Similarity: Similarly, Both poets, In the same way, Like [Poet A], [Poet B] also…

Contrast: In contrast, However, While [Poet A]…, [Poet B]…, Conversely, On the other hand

Development: [Poet B] takes this further by…, [Poet A]’s approach differs because…, This contrasts sharply with…
